claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has a more complex solute field because of its greater constituent diversity.
The complex solute field in the quinary alloy promotes dynamic strain aging during deformation.
Dynamic strain aging causes temporally fluctuating dislocation motion.
Temporally fluctuating dislocation motion manifests as serrated flow and yield-point fluctuations.
Dynamic-strain-aging features are more pronounced in the quinary alloy than in corresponding equiatomic quaternary and ternary alloys.
Reduced solute diversity in the quaternary and ternary alloys makes their pinning atmospheres less effective.
The compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys have single-phase FCC microstructures after identical thermomechanical processing.
Strain-rate-dependent tensile testing and controlled temperature variation can be used to test for activation of dynamic strain aging.
The controlled comparison spans strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1 under identical specimen preparation and thermomechanical history.
Solute-dislocation interactions periodically pin and unpin dislocations.
Slow strain rates enable the heterogeneous solute environment of the quinary alloy to transiently pin dislocations.
The quaternary and ternary alloys form fewer and less effective solute atmospheres than the quinary alloy.
Fewer and less effective solute atmospheres produce a smoother stress-strain response in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
At slow strain rates and suitable controlled temperatures, the quinary alloy will have greater stress-drop amplitude and frequency than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
At slow strain rates and suitable controlled temperatures, the quinary alloy will have larger yield-point fluctuations than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
An increase in serrated features within an appropriate temperature regime would support the proposed dynamic-strain-aging mechanism.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase FCC alloys with identical thermomechanical histories under quasi-static tensile testing near room temperature.
The temperature and strain-rate windows for optimal activation of dynamic strain aging in these alloys are not known precisely.

Statistically indistinguishable serration amplitude, serration frequency, and yield-point fluctuations between the quinary alloy and one or both lower-order alloys across the tested conditions would falsify the proposed explanation.
